paras: The Bartlesville vigilance committee ultimatum was an attempt in July 1903 by white union men in Bartlesville, Indian Territory, to drive Black laborers out of the town. Angered that a local man had hired Black workers, they formed a vigilance committee, ordered the Black men out, and threatened one at gunpoint; some fled on foot toward Kansas.

Two months earlier, the Guthrie Daily Leader had remarked that Bartlesville was "almost of the opinion that negroes are not desired in that town." The immediate cause, according to a later dispatch, was George Keeler's employment of Black men to dig a cellar, which "incensed" the white union men of the town.

On the evening of July 24, the union men organized themselves into a vigilance committee and gave the Black workers until the following night to leave. About two dozen Black workers planned to go, many setting out on foot for Kansas. A Black man from Coffeyville who had arrived that night to work in a hotel was met with guns and ordered to leave town "on pain of instant death."
Resistance came from at least one quarter: a ranchman, his cook and his porter held "the small mob of vigilants at bay with guns," after which no further violence was attempted.

By the evening of July 25 a small party of fleeing Black men had reached Coffeyville. The "better class of citizens" were reported to be out of sympathy with the movement and to have threatened "the turbulent ones" with the grand jury. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry, or the return of the workers was found.

The episode is known from a single Coffeyville, Kansas, dispatch that the Wichita Daily Eagle printed on July 26 under the headline "Incipient Race War" and the subhead "White Union Men Are Incensed by the Employment of a Negro." It called the vigilants a "small mob" and "the turbulent ones," set them against the town's "better class of citizens," and carried no editorial comment. No Black-press coverage and no report from a Bartlesville or Coffeyville paper was found.

accounts.label: Coffeyville dispatch
accounts.gist: White union men angered by Keeler's hiring of Black laborers formed a vigilance committee, gave Black workers until the night of July 25 to leave, and threatened a hotel worker with death; armed resistance by a ranchman's party checked further violence.

framing.detail: The Wichita Daily Eagle ran the dispatch as an 'Incipient Race War' caused by union men 'incensed' at Black employment, called the vigilants a 'small mob' and the 'turbulent ones', and noted that the 'better class of citizens' opposed them, without editorial comment of its own.
